## Representation of signals (4AI01) {.tiny-slide}

This course introduces various digital signal processing tools:

-  Reminders about filtering, Z-transform, and recursive filters
-  Filter synthesis methods
-  Conversion of the sampling rate
-  Short-time Fourier transform
-  Filter banks
-  Wavelets

::: {.notes}

The course introduces various digital signal processing tools that are used every day in our computers in practice, for instance

- Z-transform and recursive filters
- Conversion of sampling rate
- Short-time Fourier transform
  
and more advanced signal representations like Filter banks and wavelets
:::

. . .

These notions are related to various courses in the SPAI study track:

- multirate processing and filterbanks allow us to *pre-process signals* before applying **machine learning** methods
- they find many applications, including **denoising**, **source separation** and **inverse problems**
- time-frequency representations are essential tools in **speech processing**, **audio**, and **multimedia signal processing**

::: {.notes}
These concepts will be fundamental for your later studies, especially the ones in the SPAI track

In fact, notions are related to various courses in the SPAI study track:

- multirate processing and filterbanks allow us to *pre-process signals* before applying **machine learning** methods
- they find many applications, including **denoising**, **source separation** and **inverse problems**

# Part I: Discrete Filtering {.section-slide}

First definitions and reminders

## Signal and filters {.small-slide}

A **signal** is a sequence of real (or complex) numbers $x(n)$ for all $n \in \ZZ$

::: {.notes}
In this course, a **signal** is a sequence of real or complex numbers $x(n)$, defined for all times $n \in \ZZ$
:::

. . .

A linear and time invariant **filter** is a transform which turns a signal into another

- $x(n)$ and $y(n)$ are the *input* and *output* respectively
- for any $m \in \ZZ$, the filter transforms $x(n-m)$ into $y(n-m)$

::: {.notes}
- A filter is a transform which turns a signal into another signal, and which is both linear and invariant to translation.
- y and x are respectively the **output** and the **input** of the filter

For an LTI system, we can say that, for any integer $m$, a translation of the input by $m$ is reflected by the same translation at the output
:::

. . .

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
All filters are characterized by their **Impulse Response** $h(n)$, the transform of the impulse signal $x(n) = \delta_0(n)$

**Convolution product** describes the relationship between input and output signals
$$
    y(n) = \sum_{m\in\ZZ} h(m) x(n - m)
$$
:::

::: {.notes}
- It can be proved that all the filters are characterized by their **impulse response**, that is, the transform of the **impulse signal** $\delta_0$
- Then the general relationship between the input and the output signals is a **convolutional product** 
  - defined as the discrete integral evaluated for all values of shifts
- For the convolution product to be well defined, filter and input need to satisfy some conditions:
  - the most common is the BIBO stability, that is bounded input generates bounded output
:::

::: {.column  width="35%"}

![](https://quincyaflint.weebly.com/uploads/2/6/5/0/26500868/convolution-1-fast_orig.gif){fig-align="center"}

:::

:::

## Fourier transforms {.small-slide}

for all *normalized frequencies* $\nu\in\RR$

$$
\begin{align}
  x &\quad \overset{\mathcal{F}}{\to} & X(\eipiv)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ} x(n) e^{- 2 i \pi \nu n}\\
  h &\quad \overset{\mathcal{F}}{\to} & H(\eipiv)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ} h(n) e^{- 2 i \pi \nu n}
\end{align}
$$

where $\mathcal{F}$ denotes the **Fourier transform** 

Then, the Fourier transform of the **Convolution product** $y$ is
$$
  Y(\eipiv) = H(\eipiv) X(\eipiv)
$$

The function $H(\eipiv)$ is called the **Frequency Response** of the filter

::: {.notes}
- Signals and filters are usually studied in the Fourier domain
- If both $h$ and $x$ have well-defined Fourier transforms $H(\eipiv)$ and $X(\eipiv)$ in the variable $\nu$, which represents the normalized frequencies
- then, the convolution product can be computed as the direct product of the Fourier transforms of the filter and the input.
:::

## Causality and stability {.tiny-slide}

::: {.notes}
Beyond linearity and invariance to translation over time, we usually expect a filter to satisfy the following two conditions
:::

::: {.fragment}
### Causality

- Definition: $y(n)$ only depends on $x(k)$ , $k \leq n$
- Necessary and sufficient condition: $h(m)=0$ if $m<0$ (proof in the handout)
- Property: causal input $\implies$ causal output (proof in the handout)
- Remark: compulsory for real-time processing

::: {.notes}
- The causality is a compulsory condition when we need the filter to act in real-time.
- A filter is causal if and only if, for any input signal $x(n)$, the output $y(n)= (h \ast x)(n)$ only depends on the past samples of $x$
- Equivalently, the filter is causal if and only if $h$ is zero for negative times.
- As a consequence, if both the impulse response and the input signal are causal, then the output is causal
:::

:::

::: {.fragment}
### (BIBO) Stability

- Definition: bounded input $\implies$ bounded output
- Necessary and sufficient condition $\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty} | h(m) | < +\infty$ (i.e., $h \in l^1(\ZZ)$)
- Property: filter's frequency response is continuous (proof in the notes)
- Remark: this is numerically compulsory
  - If $x_q = x + e$, then $y_q = y + h\ast e$
  - If $h\in l^1(\ZZ)$, $\| h \ast e \|_{\infty} \leq \|h\|_1 \|e\|_\infty$, otherwise $h\ast e$ may diverge

::: {.notes}
- Next, the **stability** condition is **always** required whenever we want to numerically compute the output
- The stability means that a filter is stable if and only if, for any bounded input $x$, the output is also bounded (also known as BIBO)
- and this translates to the necessary and sufficient condition that the l1-norm of the filter is finite.
- As a consequence, the frequency response of a stable filter is always continuous
  - in fact, assume for instance that we have an input $x$ corrupted by some quantization noise $e$, due to rounding errors
  - then, by applying the filter $h$ to $x_q$, we get the output $y_q = y + h \ast e$,
  - if the filter is stable, then the residual part is bounded.
:::

:::

## Ideal filters {.small-slide}

::: {.notes}
- An ideal filter selects a given frequency range called band-pass of the input
- and rejects all other frequencies, which form the stop-band
:::

::: {.fragment}
### Low pass filter (periodic spectrum)

- Frequency response: $H(e^{2i\pi \nu}) = \begin{cases} 1 &\mbox{if } |\nu| < \nu_c \\ 0 &\mbox{if } |\nu| > \nu_c \end{cases}$
- Impulse response: $h(n) = 2 \nu_c \sinc(2\pi \nu_c n)$

::: {.notes}
- the pass-band of an ideal low-pass filter contains all frequencies lower than a given threshold, called **cut-off frequency**
- By applying the inverse DTFT to the filter, we obtain the impulse response of the filter, which is available in closed form, that is, a scaled sinus cardinal
- notice that this impulse response is continuous and infinite
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
### Exercise: band-pass filter

- Frequency response: $H(e^{2i\pi \nu}) = \begin{cases} 1 &\mbox{if } ||\nu|-\nu_0| < \nu_c \\ 0 &\mbox{if } ||\nu|-\nu_0| > \nu_c \end{cases}$
- Impulse response: $h(n)=4 \nu_c \sinc(2 \pi \nu_c n) \cos(2 \pi \nu_0 n)$

::: {.notes}
Then

- An ideal band-pass filter is characterized by two parameters, a **central frequency** $\nu_0$ and a **bandwidth** of $2\nu_c$. 
- A band-pass can be built by the differences of 2 low-pass filters and its impulse response can be easily computed in closed-form resulting in a modulated sinus cardinal
- Again, this impulse response is continuous and infinite
:::

:::

<br>

::: {.fragment}
::: {.center}
[Causality? Stability?]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
How about the causality and stability of these filters?

- For the low-pass filter, we know that the sinus cardinal is not causal and not stable (l1-norm is infinity)
  - we do not need to calculate it, just checking the frequency response:
    - it is even and real: then it cannot be causal
    - it is discontinuous: then it cannot be stable
- For the same reasons, the band-pass filter is neither causal nor stable
:::
:::

## Transient and steady states {.tiny-slide}

[For example]{.fg}

- $x(n)$ is a unit step signal: $x(n) = \vbone_{[0,+\infty[}(n)$
- $h(n)$ is an averaging filter: $h(n) = \frac1N \vbone_{[0,N-1]}(n)$

::: {.notes}
- Let's assume that the input signal is the unit step signal
- and we consider the causal averaging filter of length $N$ samples
- From before, we know that the output signal is causal, because both h and x are.
  - we would expect that averaging a constant signal like the unit step would produce $y(n)=1$ for positive samples.
:::

. . . 

We observe

- From $n=0$ to $N-2$: transient state $\quad\to$ ramp
- From $n=N-1$ to $+\infty$: steady state $\quad\to$ constant signal


::: {.notes}
- Instead, this happens only after $N-1$ samples, where $N$ is the length of the filter.
- The interval between 0 and N-2 looks like a ramp and goes from 0 to 1.
- This transition is called the **transient state** of the filter,
- which is followed by the **steady state** of the filter, where the output converges to the expected state

:::

![Transient and steady states of a causal filter](../notebooks/images/cm01_transient_steady_state.svg){fig-align="center" width=80%}

## Phase and group delays {.tiny-slide}

Frequency response: $H(\eipiv)=H_R(\nu) e^{i \phi(\nu)}$

::: {.notes}
- Let's consider the polar factorization of the frequency response of the filter $H(\eipiv)$ into real amplitude $H_R$ and phase $\phi(\nu)$.  
:::

. . . 

Phase and group delays:
<!-- [More about [Group and Phase delays](https://www.merlijnvanveen.nl/en/study-hall/165-group-delay-101)] -->

$$
\begin{cases}
  \taup(\nu_0) &= - \frac{1}{2\pi} \frac{\phi(\nu_0)}{\nu_0}\\
  \taug(\nu_0) &= - \frac{1}{2\pi} \frac{d \phi}{d \nu} (\nu_0)
\end{cases}
$$

::: {.notes}
- We will here define two quantities that measure the delays that different frequency components experience as they pass through a filter.

- These delays may be frequency dependent, so that the output signal may experience distortions 
- the **phase delay** is the time delay experienced by an individual sinusoidal frequency component
- the **group delay** is the time delay experienced by the overall envelope, or  **group** of frequencies
:::

. . .

Frequency response in the neighborhood of $\nu_0$:

$$
  H(\eipiv) \simeq H_R(\nu_0) e^{- i 2 \pi (\nu_0 \taup(\nu_0) + (\nu - \nu_0) \taug(\nu_0))}
$$

::: {.notes}
- In order to explain these definitions, let us study the filter response in the neighborhood of the frequency $\nu_0$
- Then, the filter response can be approximated using these two quantities.
- And it is easy to see by developing the Taylor expansion

**!!! Let's prove it!!!**

Let's expand the frequency response $H(\eipiv)$ around $\nu_0$ with the first-order Taylor expansion of the phase and zero-order Taylor expansion of the amplitude

$$
\begin{align}
  H(\eipiv) 
    &\simeq H_R(\nu_0) exp \left( i (\phi(\nu_0) + (\nu - \nu_0) d\phi/\ d\nu (\nu_0)) \right) \\
    &\simeq H_R(\nu_0) exp \left( i 2 \pi (\nu_0 \taup(\nu_0) + (\nu - \nu_0) \taug(\nu_0)) \right)
\end{align}
$$
::: 

. . .


Filtering of a *narrowband* signal $x$ ($y = h \ast x$) (proof in the notes):
$$
  \underbrace{x(n) = a(n) e^{i 2 \pi \nu_0 n}}_{X(\eipiv)= A\left(e^{2 i \pi (\nu - \nu_0)}\right)} 
    \quad\implies\quad y(n) \simeq H_R(\nu_0) a(n - \taug(\nu_0)) \: e^{i 2 \pi \nu_0(n - \taup(\nu_0))}
$$

::: {.notes}
Now,

- Let us now consider the output signal resulting from the convolution of $h$ with a narrow-band signal $x$.
- Remember that a narrowband signal is a signal
  - that results from the multiplication of a temporal envelope modulated by a carrier frequency 
  - and the bandwidth of the amplitude signal is assumed to be limited to the neighborhood of the zero frequency

**!!!Let us develop the math for this ...!!!**

1. Let s consider $y = h \ast x$ where the $X(\eipiv) = A(e^{i 2 \pi (\nu - \nu_0)})$
2. We have
$$
\begin{align}
  Y(\eipiv)
    &= H(\eipiv) X(\eipiv)\\
    &\simeq H_R(\nu_0) exp \left( i 2 \pi (\nu_0 \taup(\nu_0) + (\nu - \nu_0) \taug(\nu_0)) \right) \quad A(e^{i 2 \pi (\nu - \nu_0)})
\end{align}
$$
3. Then, by applying a change of variable at $\nu \to \nu + \nu_0$
$$
  Y(e^{- i 2 \pi (\nu + \nu_0)}) = H_R(\nu_0) exp \left( - i 2 \pi (\nu_0 \taup(\nu_0) + \nu \taug(\nu_0)) \right) \quad A(e^{i 2 \pi \nu})
$$
  - on the LHS: the iDTFT of $Y(e^{- i 2 \pi (\nu + \nu_0)})$ is a frequency shift <-> demodulation
  - on the RHS: is the iDTFT of a delayed signal by $\taug(\nu_0)$
1. Reverting to the time domain, $A(e^{i 2 \pi \nu}) exp (- i 2 \pi  \nu \taug(\nu_0))$
$$
y(n) e^{(- i 2 \pi \nu_0 n)} \simeq H_R(\nu_0) e^{- i 2 \pi \nu_0 \taup(\nu)} a(n - \taug(\nu_0))
$$
1. and therefore
$$
y(n) \simeq H_R(\nu_0) a(n - \taug(\nu_0)) e^{i 2 \pi \nu_0 (n - \taup(\nu_0))}
$$
:::

. . .

Linear phase filters (= the delay is constant)

::: {.notes}

- This proves that the output is also a narrowband signal, of same carrier frequency $\nu_0$ as $x(n)$,
  - with a temporal envelope which is shifted by the group delay $\taug$ w.r.t. to $x$
  - and initial phase shifted by the phase delay $\taup$ w.r.t. $x(n)$

We can see this from the delay of the envelope and the delay of the carrier modulator.

- These are two independent clocks and they need to be synced to not have distortions


As final remarks, 

- temporal waveform of the input $x$ is not distorted by the filter, if and only if the group and phase delays are equal.
- The necessary and sufficient condition for this is that $h$ is a **linear phase filter**

:::

# Part II - Z-transform {.section-slide}

##  Z-transform {.tiny-slide}

Definition: $H(z) = \sum_{n = -\infty}^{+\infty} h(n) z^{-n}$, called the **Transfer function**

- From the DTFT $H(\eipiv) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} h(n) e^{- 2 i \pi \nu n}$, we use $z = e^{2 i \pi \nu} \in \CC$

::: {.notes}
- The Z-transform is a very powerful tool to characterize the properties of discrete filters
- The Z-transform can be derived from the definition of the DTFT, by introducing the complex number $z$.
- Why can't we just use the DFT?
  - The DFT assumes an integer number of samples, defined over a circle, so its result is a periodic series
  - We can have filters that have infinite impulse responses, for which we cannot define a finite number of samples
  - so the Z-transform is like the DFT, but under the relaxed assumption of silence after the N samples
:::

. . .

Domain of convergence: $\calD = \{ z \in \CC / \sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty} |h(n)| |z|^{-n} < + \infty \}$ with shapes:

::: {.notes}
The Z-transform is also defined by a domain, called the domain of convergence

- which is related to the characteristics of the filters
- In the general cases, it looks like a ring, that is the intersection of two disks
:::

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

- **in the general case:** $\calD$ is a ring (or $\emptyset$)

. . .

- if **FIR filters:** $\calD = \CC \setminus 0$
- if **anti-causality:** $\calD$ is a disk
- if **causality:** $\calD$ is the complement of a disk

::: {.notes}
- Then if the filter is FIR, the domain spans the entire complex plane, without the origin
- if it is anti-causal, the domain is shaped like a disk
- and finally if causal, it is the complement of the disk.
::: 

:::

::: {.column}

![Z-transform](https://www.oreilly.com/api/v2/epubs/urn:orm:book:9781118393956/files/OEBPS/images/nbapp03f003.jpg){width=70%}

:::

:::


## Basic properties {.small-slide}

**Stability:** the ring $\calD$ contains the unit circle (proof in the notes)
  
  - The ZT matches the DTFT on the unit circle

::: {.notes}
- We can easily prove that $h$ is stable if and only if the ring $\calD$ contains the unit circle.
- It can be derived by applying the definition $\sum_{n\in\ZZ} | h(n) | < + \infty$ that implies $|z|=1$
:::

. . .

Linearity: $a_1 h_1 + a_2 h_2 \to a_1 H_1 + a_2 H_2$ with ($\calD \supset \calD_1 \cap \calD_2$)


::: {.notes}
- Then, we have a set of properties that are similar to the ones of the DTFT
- we have the linearity of the transformation
:::


. . .

Delay: $y(n) = x(n-k) \iff Y(z)=z^{-k} X(z)$


::: {.notes}

- Applying a delay is equivalent to multiplying by $z^{-k}$

:::


. . .

Convolution product:

  - if $y = h\ast x$, then $Y(z)=H(z)X(z)$, $\calD_y \supset \calD_h \cap \calD_x$


::: {.notes}

The convolution product translates into a product in the transformed domain

:::

. . .

Insertion of zeros: $Y(z) = X(z^L) \iff y(nL) = x(n)$, $y=0$ elsewhere


::: {.notes}
Then, adding zeros between consecutive samples doesn't change the signal content: the spectrum is squeezed and repeated.
:::

. . .

Inverse filter

  - if $h \ast h_i = \delta$, then $H(z)H_i(z) = 1$ for $z \in \calD_h \cap \calD_{h_i}$


::: {.notes}

Finally, as a consequence of the convolution product, the inverse filter is the one that results in the identity when the two transforms are multiplied.

:::


## Example of ZT {.small-slide}


::: {.notes}

Here are a few examples of useful Z-transforms.

We have:

- the identity filter
- the step filter
- the rectangular filter, that is, the ideal low-pass filter

:::

- $h(n) = \delta(n)$ $\implies$ $H(z) = 1$, $\quad\forall z \in \CC$
- $h(n) = 1_{[0,+\infty[}(n)$ $\implies$ $H(z) = \frac{1}{1 - z^{-1}}$, $\quad\forall |z| > 1$
- $h(n) = 1_{[0,N-1]}(n) \implies H(z) = \frac{1 - z^{-N}}{1 - z^{-1}}$, $\quad\forall |z| \neq 0$

. . .


AR1 filter:

  - $h(n) = \begin{cases}a^n &\text{if } n\geq 0 \\ 0 &\text{if } n < 0\end{cases} \implies H(z)= \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}}$ with $\calD = \{ z \in \CC / |z| > |a|\}$
  

::: {.notes}
And autoregressive filters, which are important filters that will be later defined as **recursive filters**

For instance, here, we have autoregressive filter of order 1 (also known as AR1 filter) 

- Let be $h(n)$ defined as $a^n$ for positive samples and zeros otherwise
- The impulse response is causal, so we already know that the domain of convergence is the complement of a disk of radius $|a|$

Then
- The filter is stable $\iff$ the domain contains the unit circle, that is, $|a| < 1$. 
- Which makes sense, as for $|a| < 1$ the series converges

:::

. . . 

- $h(n) = \begin{cases}-a^n &\text{if } n< 0 \\ 0 &\text{if } n \geq 0\end{cases} \implies H(z)= \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}}$  with $\calD = \{ z \in \CC / |z| < |a|\}$
  

::: {.notes}

Then we have the **anti-causal** version, defined similarly, but with negative coefficients and for negative samples

- we can notice that the form of the Z-transform is the same
- but the domain of convergence is different, which is now the interior of the disk with radius $|a|$
:::

## Autoregressive filter of order 1 {.center .small-slide}

::: {.callout}
## Autoregressive filter of order 1

- Transfer function: $H(z) = \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}}$
- Input/output relationship : $y(n) - a y(n-1) = x(n)$

:::


::: {.notes}

- Since the causal and anti-causal AR1 filter have the same transfer function, 
- then we have two **implementations** of the same filter
- which in the time domain can be written in a recursive way as here
- in an equation that is called **input/output relationship**
:::

. . .

|                             |       Forward recursion       |   Backward recursion              |
|-----------------------------|:-----------------------------:|:---------------------------------:|
| Implementation              | $y(n)=a y(n-1) + x(n)$        | $y(n)= \frac{y(n+1) - x(n+1)}{a}$ |
| IR ($x(n)=\delta_0(n)$)     | $h(n) = a^n \vbone_{\{n\geq 0\}}$  | $h(n) = -a^n \vbone_{\{n< 0\}}$      |
| Domain                      | $\{ z \in \CC / |z| > |a| \}$ | $\{ z \in \CC / |z| < |a| \}$     |
| Properties                  | causal , stable if $|a| < 1$  | anti-causal, stable if $|a| > 1$  |


::: {.notes}

The forward recursion is defined for increasing times

- this is the causal implementation
- and it is numerically stable if and only if $|a|<1$
- that is, any error in the computation of $y(n-1)$ is reduced by a factor $|a|$ in the computation of $y(n)$

The backward recursion, or anticausal implementation, is defined instead for decreasing times

- it is numerically stable if and only if $|a|>1$,
- and now any error in the computation of $y(n+1)$ is reduced by a factor 1 over $|a|$ in $y(n)$

:::

. . .


::: {.notes}

In this simple case, looking at $a$ is sufficient to know which implementation to use.

But this will be now generalized to the general context of **recursive filters**

:::


# Part III - Recursive filters {.section-slide}

## Recursive filters {.small-slide}

Input-output relationship

$$
\sum_{k=0}^N a_k y(n-k) = \sum_{k=0}^M b_k x(n - k)
$$


::: {.notes}

Recursive filters generalize the notion of the AR1 filter of the previous section

The I/O relationship relates the samples of both the output signal $y$ and the input signal $x$
:::

. . .

Computation of the output (causal implementation)
$$
y(n) = \frac{1}{a_0} \left[  \sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k x(n - k) - \sum_{k=1}^N a_k y(n - k) \right]
$$


::: {.notes}

Note that this relation defines a filter 

- where the output samples are linear functions of the input samples

Therefore we can define a filter whose impulse response looks like this.

The I/O relationship admits several implementations

- this one is the causal one

:::

. . .

Transfer function

$$
  H(z) 
    = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^M b_k z^{-k}}{\sum_{k=0}^N a_k z^{-k}}
    = \frac{b_0}{a_0} \frac{\prod_{k=1}^M  (1 - c_k z^{-1})}{ \prod_{k=1}^N (1 - d_k z^{-1})}
$$


::: {.notes}

The transfer function can be always expressed as a simple function of the coefficients $a_k$ and $b_k$ as shown here

- where $c_k$ are known as the **zeros** and the $d_k$ are known as the **poles** of the filter.

:::


## Example of recursive filters {.small-slide}

[Auto-regression filters (if $M=0$, AR of order $N$)]{.fg}

$$
  y(n) = \frac{b_0}{a_0} x(n) - \sum_{k=1}^N \frac{a_k}{a_0} y(n - k)
$$

[Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters]{.fg}

- If $N=0$, FIR filter of length $M+1$
  $$
    h(n) = \begin{cases} \frac{b_n}{a_0} &\text{if } n=0,\ldots,M\\ 0 &\text{otherwise}\end{cases}
  $$
- Causal filters, unconditionally stable
- If the IR is symmetric or anti-symmetric, the phase is linear


::: {.notes}

There are two particular classes of recursive filters which are widely used in signal processing 

- the AR filters
- and the Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters

The AR filters, are recursive with no zeros 

- The I/O relationship simplifies to this formulation
- These filters are widely used in speech processing, because they can model the vocal tract

The FIR filters are recursive filters with no poles

- their impulse response can be simply written as this
- they are widely used in signal processing, because they are stable and causal by construction
- in addition, if the IR is symmetric (or anti-symmetric), their phase is linear
:::

## Recursive filters {.small-slide}

### Transfer function of a recursive filter
$$
  H(z) 
    = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^M b_k z^{-k}}{\sum_{k=0}^N a_k z^{-k}}
    = \frac{b_0}{a_0} \frac{\prod_{k=1}^M  (1 - c_k z^{-1})}{ \prod_{k=1}^N (1 - d_k z^{-1})}
$$

Domain of convergence: $\calD$ is a ring bounded by 2 poles, with no pole inside of it

- **Stable** filter $\to$ $\calD$ is the largest ring containing the unit circle and no pole
- **Stable and causal** filters $\to$ whose poles are all strictly inside the unit circle
- if the $a_k$ and $b_k$ are real, the poles and zeros are either real, or form conjugate pairs


::: {.notes}

The transfer function of a recursive filter tells us some properties of the domain of convergence of the filter

- the domain $\calD$ is a ring, bounded by two poles, with no pole inside
- there is an **unique stable** implementation if and only if there is no pole on the unit circle
- there is a **unique stable and causal** implementation if and only if all poles are strictly inside the unit circle
- if all the coefficients $a_k$ and $b_k$ are real, the poles and zeros are either real, or form conjugate pairs

:::

## Interactive visualization

<iframe src="widgets/cm01_roc-explorer.html?cols=2,2,3" width="100%" height="100%"
        style="border:none;" loading="lazy"></iframe>

::: {.notes}

Suggested visualization:

1. 2 poles inside the circle $\to$ only the outer ring contains the unit circle
2. Push $d_2$ past 1 $\to$ now the middle ring is the stable one
  - only the mixed implementation is stable
  - stability and causality are separate 
3. Push both poles outside (1.4, 1.6) $\to$  the inner circle becomes stable
  - the filter is purely anti-causal
  - stability is not only "decaying" on the right

:::


## Computation of the IR from the ZT {.tiny-slide}

::: {.small}

::: {.notes}

In this slide we recall the methodology to compute the impulse response of a filter given its Z-transform

For instance we have this filter

:::

::: {layout=[3,2] .small}
\

$\quad\quad H(z) = \frac{1}{1 - \frac52 z^{-1}  + z^{-2}}$
:::

. . .

::: {layout=[3,2] .small}
1. If necessary, extract from $H(z)$ a term in $z^n$, so that numerator and denominator only contain negative powers of $z$ plus a constant

Nothing to extract: already a ratio in $z^{-n}$
:::

::: {.notes}

The first step rewrite the filter in terms of negative powers of $z$

so here there is nothing to do as it is already in the correct form

:::

. . .

::: {layout=[3,2] .small}
2. Factorize the numerator and denominator as product of monomials of $z^{-1}$

$H(z) = \frac{1}{(1 - 2z^{-1})(1 - \tfrac12 z^{-1})}$
:::

::: {.notes}
Second, Factorize the numerator and denominator as product of monomials of $z^{-1}$
:::

. . .

::: {layout=[3,2] .small}
3. Compute the partial fraction decomposition of $H(z)$ as a function of $z^{-1}$

$H(z) = \frac{4/3}{1-2z^{-1}} - \frac{1/3}{1-\frac12 z^{-1}}$
:::

::: {.notes}
Then we need to compute the decomposition as a function of $z^{-1}$
:::

. . .

::: {layout=[3,2] .small}
::: {}
4. Expand these fractions in power series

  - of $z^{-1}$ if we compute the causal IR, or if we compute the stable IR and the pole is inside the unit circle
  - of $z$ if we compute the *anti*-causal IR, or if we compute the stable IR and the pole is outside of the unit circle 
:::

::: {}
ROC: $\tfrac12 < |z| < 2$:

<br>

$\frac{1}{1-\tfrac12 z^{-1}} = \sum_{n\ge 0} 2^{-n} z^{-n}$

$\frac{1}{1-2z^{-1}} = -\sum_{n\ge 1} 2^{-n} z^{n}$
::: 

:::

::: {.notes}
Then we expand this fraction into power series, each for the causal and anti-causal part
:::

. . .

::: {layout=[3,2] .small}
1. Identify the resulting expression with $H(z) = \sum_{n\in \ZZ} h(n)z^{-n}$


::: {.small}
$h(n) = \begin{cases}-\frac23 \left(\frac12\right)^{n+1} & n \ge 0\\ -\frac23 \, 2^{n+1} & n < 0\end{cases}$ 
:::

::: {.notes}

And finally we can rewrite the filter by matching with the expression of the Z-transform

:::

:::

:::

## Geometric interpretation of the FR {.small-slide}

### Example (AR2 filter):
$$
H(z) = \frac1{1 + a_1 z^{-1} + a_2 z^{-2}} = \frac1{(1 - p z^{-1}) (1 - p^\ast z^{-1})}
$$


::: {.notes}

The shape of the Frequency response of a recursive filter can be easily deduced from the expansion of its transfer function.

Let's consider this causal AR2 filter, where we assume the coefficients form two poles in a conjugate pair.

:::

. . .

<br>

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

$PM = |p - z|$, $QM = |p^\ast - z|$:

$$
\begin{align}
  |H(z)| &= \frac1{PM \times QM} \\ \\
  \arg H(z) &= 2 \arg(OM) \\
            &\quad- \arg(PM) - \arg(QM)
\end{align}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

<iframe src="widgets/cm01_geometric_fr.html" width="100%" height="380"
        style="border:none;" loading="lazy"></iframe>

:::

:::

::: {.notes}

Let

- M be the coordinate of the point in the Z-plane representing the complex number $z$
- P be the point for the pole $p$
- and Q the point for its conjugate $p^\ast$

Then PM and QM are the distances between these two points

We can then plot the magnitude of the frequency response $|H(\eipiv)|$ as function of $z = \eipiv$

Moving $\nu$ from 0 to $\frac12$, M travels over the unit circle counter-clockwise, from 1 to $-1$

When M is close to P, the distance PM is small, then the magnitude of $H(z)$ is high, producing a resonance peak.

:::

## Spectral factorization {.small-slide .blurred}

Factorization of the transfer function

$$
  H(z) 
    = \frac{b_0}{a_0} \frac{\prod_{k=1}^M  (1 - c_k z^{-1})}{ \prod_{k=1}^N (1 - d_k z^{-1})}
$$

Amplitude response ($z = \eipiv$)

$$
  | H(\eipiv) |^2 = H(z) H(1/z^\ast) 
    = \left| \frac{b_0}{a_0} \right|^2 \frac{\prod_{k=1}^M  (1 - c_k z^{-1})(1 - c_k^\ast z)}{ \prod_{k=1}^N (1 - d_k z^{-1})(1 - d_k^\ast z)}
$$

- Poles with $|z| < 1$: stability + causality
- Zeros with $|z| < 1$: minimal phase 

## All-pass filters {.small-slide .blurred}

Definition: $H(z) = \prod_{k=1}^N \frac{z^{-1} - c_k^\ast}{1 - c_k z^{-1}}$ where $| c_k | < 1$ $\forall k$

$H(z)$ is all-pass, *causal* and stable

Properties (if $y = h \ast x$):

- $\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} | x(n) |^2 = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty} | y(n) |^2$
- An all-pass filter is such that $\sum_{n=-\infty}^{N} |x(n)|^2 \geq \sum_{n=-\infty}^{N} |y(n)|^2$  
  Proof hint: $x_N(n) = x(n) \times  1_{]-\infty, N]}(n)$

## Spectral factorization {.small-slide .blurred}

![](images/fig9.svg)

## Minimal phase filters {.small-slide .blurred}

- Definition: filter whose poles and zeros are all inside the unit circle
- Any causal and stable recursive filter is the product of an all-pass filter and a minimal phase filter
- Properties (if $g$ is causal and stable, $y = g \ast x$ and $|G| = |G_m|$)
  - The inverse filter is also stable and causal
  - $\sum_{n = -\infty}^{+\infty} | y(n) |^2 \geq \sum_{n=-\infty}^N |y(n)|^2$
  - $g_m$ has the lowest group delay

## Minimal phase filters {.small-slide .blurred}

# Part IV - FIR filters: window method {.section-slide}

## Window methods {.tiny-slide}

**Example:** FIR of the ideal low-pass filter $h(n)= 2 \nu_c \sinc(2 \pi \nu_c n)$

- The response is IIR, non-causal, non-stable

::: {layout="[100,-20,100]" layout-valign="center"}

![](./images/fig39.svg){style="height:120px" fig-align="right"}

![](./images/fig38.svg){style="height:120px" fig-align="left"}

:::

  
::: {.notes}

Let's consider an ideal low-pass filter now

which has a flat response up to the cut-off frequency, and of course, it is symmetric

We know the impulse response in closed form, and we know that it is infinite, non-causal and non-stable

The question is then: how can we compute the FIR version of it?
:::


. . . 

Synthesis of a Type I causal FIR filter

- Truncation and temporal shift

::: {layout="[100,-20,100]" layout-valign="center"}

![](./images/fig40.svg){style="height:120px" fig-align="right"}

![](./images/fig41.svg){style="height:120px" fig-align="left"}

:::


::: {.notes}

We can build a **finite** impulse response by multiplying this by a window with finite temporal support, in the time domain

We then obtain an FIR filter, that we can make causal by applying a temporal shift

The spectral result is a convolution of the Fourier transform of the ideal response and the Fourier transform of the window

And in the figure we can see the impulse and frequency response of the resulting FIR filter synthesized by the window method

As you notice, we get some spurious oscillations, known as the Gibbs effect, due to the truncation of the filter

:::


## Gibbs phenomenon {.small-slide}

::: {.r-stack}

![](images/fig42.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig43.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig44.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig45.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig46.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig47.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig48.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig49.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig50.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig51.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

:::


::: {.notes}

we can see here the actual visualization of what is happening under the hood

We have a product of the window (an ideal rect) and the impulse response of the ideal low pass filter (a sinc)

Then the product in the time domain is the convolution in the frequency domain

so as we convolve an oscillating signal with the rect we notice ripple appears

The dots show the output of the convolution

This is known as the Gibbs effect

:::


## Gibbs phenomenon {.small-slide}

![](images/fig51.svg){width=50% fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}

We can notice two effects

- **ripples** appear in the passband and in the stopband, which are related to the sidelobes of the Fourier transform of the window.
  - this means that the **stopband attenuation** is related to the **level of these sidelobes**
- the obtained filter is no longer infinitely selective: 
  - a **transition band** appears between the passband and the stopband. 
    - the width of this transition band (that is the **filter selectivity**) is related to the **width** of the **main lobe** of the transform of the window
:::


## Choice of a suitable window {.small-slide}

::: {.notes}

This brings us to the question of the choice of good windows, ideally without ripples that can well approximate an ideal low-pass filter

- to synthesize FIR filters.

The selection of the window's shape is based on a trade-off between the level of the sidelobes and the width of the main lobe.

:::

$$
  h(n) = 2 \nu_c \sinc(2 \pi \nu_c n) w(n)
$$

where $w(n)$ is a symmetric window of finite support

![](images/fig53.svg){width=50% fig-align="center"}


## Notable windows {.small-slide}


::: {.panel-tabset}
## [Rectangular window]{.small}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
<br>
$$
  w(n) = \vbone_{[0,P-1]}(n)
$$

- width: $\frac{2}{P}$
- second lobe: -13 dB
- decrease rate: -6 dB / octave

:::

::: {.column}

![](images/fig16.svg)

:::

:::

## [Bartlett window]{.small}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column .small}
<br>
$$
  w(n) = 1 - \left| \frac{2n}{P-1} - 1 \right|
$$

- width: $\frac4P$
- second lobe: -26 dB
- decrease rate: -12 dB / octave

:::

::: {.column}

![](images/fig17.svg)

:::

:::

## [Hann window]{.small}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
<br>
$$
  w(n) = 0.5 - 0.5 \cos \left( 2 \pi \frac{n}{P-1} \right)
$$

- width: $\frac4P$
- second lobe: -31 dB
- decrease rate: -18 dB / octave

:::

::: {.column}

![](images/fig18.svg)

:::

:::

## [Hamming window]{.small}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
<br>
$$
  w(n) = 0.54 - 0.46 \cos \left( 2 \pi \frac{n}{P-1} \right)
$$

- width: $\frac4P$
- second lobe: -41 dB
- decrease rate: -6 dB / octave
:::

::: {.column}

![Hamming window](images/fig19.svg)

::: 

:::

## [Blackman window]{.small}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
<br>

::: {.smaller}
$$
  w(n) = 0.4266 - 0.4965 \cos\left( 2 \pi \frac{n}{P-1} \right) + 0.076  \cos \left( 4 \pi \frac{n}{P-1} \right)
$$
:::



- width: $\frac6P$
- second lobe: -57 dB
- decrease rate: -18 dB / octave
:::

::: {.column}

![](images/fig20.svg)

::: 

:::

:::


::: {.notes}

In this slide we can compare different window functions that provide a trade-off between

- ripples of the side lobes
- and the width of the main lobe

We have

- the ideal rectangular windows
- the Bartlett window or triangular window
- the Hann window
- the Hamming window
- and the Blackman window

which one do we use in practice? Well, this is a question you will be able to answer at the end of this course
:::


## Window method {.small-slide}

[Advantages]{.fg}

- Stability, causality
- Linear phase filter if symmetric window

::: {.notes}

So, to conclude this first lesson, let's summarize some properties of the window methods

This method is used 

- synthesize FIR filters
- and guarantee the stability and causality of the result

and if the window is symmetric, we are guaranteed a linear phase filter, which is desirable to maintain the signal in the passband

:::

. . .

[Drawbacks]{.fg}

- the transition bands are widened
- the spurious ripples
  - are due to side lobes
  - do not have a constant amplitude
  - are the same in passband and stopband

::: {.notes}

On the other side...

- the transition bands of the results of the ideal filter are widened
- and spurious ripples due to sidelobes appear 
  - characterized by non constant amplitude both in the pass and stop bands
  - leading to artifacts in the resulting filter

In the following lecture we will see other methods to synthesize FIR filters
:::
